title: Sampling and Survey Methods
subject: Statistics

cards.prompt: What is Target Population? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A target population is the set of units about which a study intends to draw conclusions, defined by explicit membership and time boundaries. It can differ from the units actually reachable through the sampling frame.
required_concepts: Explicit set of intended inference units.
Membership and reference time are specified.
major_error_concepts: Defining the population only as the people who happened to respond.

cards.prompt: What is Finite Population? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A finite population contains a fixed finite number N of units for the reference period. In design-based inference, their values are treated as fixed and randomness comes from how the sample is selected.
required_concepts: Finite set of N units.
Selection supplies design-based randomness.
major_error_concepts: Assuming design-based analysis requires the population itself to be an IID random sample.

cards.prompt: What is Sample? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sample is the subset or selected collection of population units observed under a sampling procedure. Its realized composition differs from the sampling design, which specifies how possible samples could be selected.
required_concepts: Selected units, distinct from the selection rule.
major_error_concepts: Equating one realized sample with the full sampling design.

cards.prompt: What is Sampling Unit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sampling unit is an entity eligible for selection at a specified stage, such as a school or household. It need not be the final entity whose outcome is analyzed.
required_concepts: Selectable entity at a stated sampling stage.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the sampling unit must always equal the analysis unit.

cards.prompt: What is Observation and Analysis Units? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An observation unit is the entity on which a measurement is recorded; an analysis unit is the entity represented by the inferential target. A respondent may report measurements for other observation units, so these roles should be distinguished.
required_concepts: Measurement, analysis, and respondent roles can differ.
accepted_variants: Unit of observation versus unit of analysis.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the person answering a household survey is necessarily the unit for every recorded variable.

cards.prompt: What is Sampling Frame? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sampling frame is the operational list or selection mechanism from which candidate units can be sampled. Its coverage of the target population must account for excluded, duplicated, outdated, or ineligible entries.
required_concepts: Operational basis for sample selection.
Frame coverage is not automatic.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every available contact list perfectly covers the target population.

cards.prompt: What is Coverage Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Coverage error arises when the frame and target population do not align, including missing eligible units or including ineligible ones. It is distinct from eligible sampled units failing to respond.
required_concepts: Mismatch between frame coverage and target population.
Distinct from nonresponse.
major_error_concepts: Calling frame omissions ordinary sampling variation that necessarily vanishes with a larger sample.

cards.prompt: What is Survey Estimand? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An estimand is the precisely defined population quantity a study aims to estimate. It specifies the variable, population, reference period, and summary, rather than merely naming a statistical procedure.
required_concepts: Target quantity with population and variable definition.
accepted_variants: Quantity of scientific or descriptive interest.
major_error_concepts: Calling a software command the estimand without naming the target quantity.

cards.prompt: What is Population Total? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A finite-population total is T=sum over all N units of y_i. It counts the aggregate quantity in the specified population and differs from a total calculated only over the sample.
required_concepts: Sum over every population unit.
major_error_concepts: Reporting an unweighted sample total as the population total without a valid expansion.

cards.prompt: What is Population Mean? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A finite-population mean is the population total divided by N. Its target is an average per population unit, so an estimate of a total must be normalized appropriately to estimate the mean.
required_concepts: Population sum divided by population size.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by the realized sample size when converting the actual population total to a population mean.

cards.prompt: What is Population Proportion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A population proportion is the mean of a zero-one indicator for a defined characteristic. Its numerator counts eligible units with that characteristic and its denominator counts all units in the target population or stated domain.
required_concepts: Mean of a binary indicator.
Denominator matches the target population.
accepted_variants: Population fraction or prevalence of a defined attribute.
major_error_concepts: Changing the denominator without changing the reported estimand.

cards.prompt: What is Census? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A census seeks observations from every unit in the target population. It removes sample-selection variation only when enumeration is complete, but coverage, nonresponse, measurement, and processing errors can still occur.
required_concepts: Attempted complete enumeration.
Nonsampling errors remain possible.
major_error_concepts: Claiming any census necessarily measures the population without error.

cards.prompt: What is Sampling Design? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sampling design is a probability rule assigning chances to possible samples. It specifies stages, replacement, selection probabilities, and constraints needed to understand an estimator's sampling behavior.
required_concepts: Probability distribution over possible samples.
major_error_concepts: Treating an undocumented realized sample as a fully specified probability design.

cards.prompt: What is Probability Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Probability sampling selects units through a known random mechanism with positive inclusion probabilities for the target units. It supports design-based inference when the design and response issues are handled appropriately.
required_concepts: Known random selection and positive inclusion probabilities.
major_error_concepts: Calling a voluntary opt-in sample a probability sample solely because it is large.

cards.prompt: What is Nonprobability Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A nonprobability sample does not give every target unit a known selection probability through a documented random design. Generalization then relies on additional modeling, selection assumptions, or external information rather than design randomization alone.
required_concepts: Unknown or nonrandom selection probabilities.
Population inference needs additional assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming demographic resemblance alone supplies known inclusion probabilities.

cards.prompt: What is Simple Random Sampling Without Replacement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Simple random sampling without replacement selects n distinct units so every subset of size n has equal probability. Each unit has inclusion probability n/N, but selections are not independent because the sample size is fixed.
required_concepts: Equal probability for all n-unit subsets.
Distinct selections with inclusion probability n/N.
major_error_concepts: Assuming independent selection indicators in fixed-size sampling without replacement.

cards.prompt: What is Simple Random Sampling With Replacement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Simple random sampling with replacement takes independent uniform draws from the population, allowing repeats. Draw probability is 1/N, while a unit's probability of appearing at least once across n draws is generally not n/N.
required_concepts: Independent equal-probability draws, repeats allowed.
Draw probability differs from eventual inclusion probability.
major_error_concepts: Confusing per-draw probability with the probability of ever being selected.

cards.prompt: What is Inclusion Probability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The first-order inclusion probability pi_i is the probability that unit i belongs to the final sample. It is a design probability, not the unit's realized zero-one membership or necessarily its per-draw selection chance.
required_concepts: Probability of final sample inclusion.
major_error_concepts: Substituting a draw probability for inclusion probability in a design where they differ.

cards.prompt: What is Joint Inclusion Probability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The second-order inclusion probability pi_ij is the probability that both units i and j are included. Joint inclusion probabilities determine selection dependence and enter design-based variance formulas.
required_concepts: Probability of joint inclusion.
Encodes dependence between selections.
major_error_concepts: Assuming pi_ij always equals pi_i times pi_j under without-replacement sampling.

cards.prompt: What is Base Sampling Weight? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A base sampling weight is 1/pi_i for a unit with positive inclusion probability. It expands the selected unit according to its representation under the design, before separate nonresponse or calibration adjustments.
required_concepts: Inverse inclusion probability.
Base weight precedes later adjustments.
accepted_variants: Design weight or inverse-probability sampling weight.
major_error_concepts: Using inclusion probability itself as the expansion weight.

cards.prompt: What is Inclusion Indicator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sample inclusion indicator I_i equals one if unit i is selected and zero otherwise. Its design expectation is pi_i, allowing sampled estimators to be written as sums across the fixed population.
required_concepts: Binary selection indicator with expectation pi_i.
major_error_concepts: Treating I_i as a continuously varying selection probability.

cards.prompt: What is Design Expectation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Design expectation averages over possible samples drawn from the stated design while holding finite-population values fixed. It differs from expectation over a model that randomly generates the population values.
required_concepts: Average over random sample selection.
Population values held fixed.
major_error_concepts: Replacing the actual sampling design with an IID population model without stating the change.

cards.prompt: What is Design Unbiasedness? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An estimator is design-unbiased when its expectation over the sampling design equals the finite-population estimand. This does not mean every realized estimate is correct or that nonresponse cannot introduce bias.
required_concepts: Design expectation equals target.
major_error_concepts: Claiming unbiasedness means zero error in each sample.

cards.prompt: What is Sampling Variance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sampling variance is the variance of an estimator across samples generated by the design. It measures random selection variability around the design expectation, not all sources of survey error.
required_concepts: Repeated-design variability of the estimator.
major_error_concepts: Calling sampling variance a complete measure of coverage and measurement bias.

cards.prompt: What is Standard Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A standard error is the square root of an estimator's variance, usually estimated from the sample and design information. It is measured in the estimator's units, unlike the variance.
required_concepts: Square root of estimator variance.
major_error_concepts: Confusing standard error of a mean with standard deviation of individual outcomes.

cards.prompt: What is Sampling Bias? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sampling bias is systematic distortion arising when selection or frame coverage does not support the intended population inference. Increasing the size of a systematically selective convenience sample does not by itself eliminate that bias.
required_concepts: Systematic selection-related distortion.
Larger samples do not automatically remove selection bias.
major_error_concepts: Treating a very large convenience sample as automatically representative.

cards.prompt: What is Mean Squared Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Mean squared error is expected squared deviation of an estimator from its target. When finite, it equals variance plus squared bias, so low variance alone does not guarantee accurate estimation.
required_concepts: MSE equals variance plus bias squared.
major_error_concepts: Calling a highly precise but badly biased estimator necessarily accurate.

cards.prompt: What is Design Consistency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Design consistency means an estimator approaches the target in probability along a specified sequence of growing populations and sampling designs. It is an asymptotic property and does not imply exact unbiasedness in a finite sample.
required_concepts: Convergence under a stated design asymptotic sequence.
major_error_concepts: Equating consistency with exact finite-sample unbiasedness.

cards.prompt: What is Finite-Population Correction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The finite-population correction reflects reduced variance when sampling without replacement takes a substantial fraction f=n/N of a finite population. In the usual SRS mean variance formula it contributes the factor 1-f.
required_concepts: Without-replacement variance reduction depends on sample fraction.
major_error_concepts: Applying the same correction automatically to independent with-replacement draws.

cards.prompt: What is SRS Mean Variance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Under SRS without replacement, Var(ybar)=(1-n/N)S squared/n, where S squared uses denominator N-1 in the population. Replacing S squared by the sample variance gives the usual unbiased variance estimate when n exceeds one.
required_concepts: Correct SRS mean variance with FPC.
Variance convention is specified.
major_error_concepts: Omitting the sample fraction when it is large while claiming the exact finite-population formula.

cards.prompt: What is SRS Total Estimator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Under fixed-size SRS, the expansion estimator for a total is N times the sample mean. Its variance is N squared times the sample-mean variance when N is known.
required_concepts: Estimated total N times sample mean.
Variance scales by N squared.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying the mean variance by N rather than N squared.

cards.prompt: What is SRS Proportion Estimator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sample proportion under SRS is the sample mean of a binary indicator. Its uncertainty follows the corresponding mean-variance calculation, with finite-population and small-count issues considered as appropriate.
required_concepts: Indicator mean with design-aware variance.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a proportion estimate has zero uncertainty because each observation is only zero or one.

cards.prompt: What is Design-Based Confidence Interval? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A design-based confidence interval uses an estimator and a design-appropriate uncertainty method to achieve repeated-sampling coverage under its assumptions. The fixed finite-population parameter is not repeatedly randomized by the interval procedure.
required_concepts: Repeated-design coverage for a fixed target.
Appropriate uncertainty method required.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a realized frequentist interval assigns a posterior probability to the fixed parameter without a Bayesian model.

cards.prompt: What is Margin of Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A margin of error is the half-width of a stated interval, often a critical value times a standard error. It depends on coverage level, design, and estimator, and usually excludes nonsampling biases.
required_concepts: Interval half-width under specified assumptions.
Not total survey error.
major_error_concepts: Reporting a margin of error as a bound on every possible survey bias.

cards.prompt: What is Precision-Based Sample-Size Planning? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Precision-based sample-size planning chooses n to reach a target interval width or estimation error under stated variability, design, and coverage assumptions. It is distinct from planning power to detect a specified effect.
required_concepts: Choose n for target estimation precision.
Declare variability and design assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Calling any hypothesis-test power calculation a precision calculation without relating it to interval width.

cards.prompt: What is Proportion Sample-Size Formula? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a large-population SRS proportion, the normal-approximation planning formula is n approximately z squared times p(1-p) divided by e squared for half-width e. Using p=0.5 maximizes this variance term, not every possible source of survey error.
required_concepts: Correct approximate proportion planning formula.
p=0.5 is conservative for the binomial variance term.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the formula automatically covers clustering, nonresponse bias, or arbitrary nonprobability selection.

cards.prompt: What is Nonresponse Allowance in Planning? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sample-size inflation for nonresponse divides the required number of completed responses by an assumed response fraction. It budgets invitations or selections but does not remove bias from selective response.
required_concepts: Required completions divided by expected response fraction.
More invitations do not eliminate nonresponse bias.
major_error_concepts: Claiming inflating the sample makes nonresponse ignorable.

cards.prompt: What is Design Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A design effect is the ratio of an estimator's variance under the actual design to a stated reference design, commonly same-size SRS. It is estimator-specific and can reflect clustering, stratification, and weighting.
required_concepts: Variance ratio relative to an explicit reference design.
Depends on estimator.
major_error_concepts: Treating design effect as one universal constant for every variable and estimate.

cards.prompt: What is Effective Sample Size? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A design-effect effective sample size is approximately n/DEFF relative to the chosen SRS comparison. It summarizes precision equivalence, not the literal count of independent respondents or protection against bias.
required_concepts: Precision-equivalent sample size relative to stated design.
Does not quantify selection bias.
major_error_concepts: Calling an effective sample size a proof of representativeness.

cards.prompt: What is Power-Based Sample Planning? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Power-based sample planning chooses a design and sample size to detect a specified alternative with stated type-I error and power. Effect size, outcome variability, clustering, and allocation affect the calculation.
required_concepts: Plan detection probability for a specified effect and test.
major_error_concepts: Assuming power is defined without an alternative effect size.

cards.prompt: What is Stratified Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Stratified sampling divides the population into nonoverlapping exhaustive strata and samples within each stratum. It can improve precision or ensure subgroup coverage when allocation and weights reflect the design.
required_concepts: Partition population and sample within each stratum.
major_error_concepts: Confusing strata sampled throughout the population with selecting only some clusters.

cards.prompt: Give a stratified estimator of the finite-population mean and state when ordinary within-stratum sample means are justified.
cards.definition: If known stratum sizes N_h partition a population of size N, combine stratum mean estimators as Ybar_hat_st=sum_h (N_h/N) Ybar_hat_h. Under SRS within each stratum, Ybar_hat_h is the ordinary stratum sample mean and the combination is design-unbiased. Other within-stratum designs require estimators justified for those designs. Population shares, not sample shares, determine the target population mean; equal stratum weights are appropriate only for equal population sizes or a different explicitly stated target.
required_concepts: Combine stratum mean estimates using known population shares N_h/N.
Ordinary stratum sample means have the stated unbiasedness under within-stratum SRS, not arbitrary selection.
Distinguish population shares from equal weights or sample shares.
major_error_concepts: For any unequal-probability design within strata, the unweighted stratum sample means are automatically design-unbiased, so only the final stratum weights matter.

cards.prompt: State the variance of a stratified mean under independent SRS without replacement within strata, and how it is estimated.
cards.definition: For independent SRS-without-replacement samples in strata h, let W_h=N_h/N and S_h^2=sum_(i in h)(y_i-Ybar_h)^2/(N_h-1), for strata with N_h>1. Then Var(Ybar_hat_st) is the sum of W_h^2(1-n_h/N_h)S_h^2/n_h over noncensus strata; censused strata, including single-unit strata, contribute zero separately. For noncensus strata with n_h>1, replacing S_h^2 by the usual sample variance gives the corresponding unbiased variance estimator. Independence across strata removes cross-covariance terms.
required_concepts: Sum W_h^2(1-n_h/N_h)S_h^2/n_h for independent within-stratum SRSWOR.
Each stratum has its own FPC and variance with denominator N_h-1.
Use sample-variance replacement only where it is estimable; census contributions are zero.
major_error_concepts: Add the unweighted stratum variances and apply one common FPC even when their population shares and sampling fractions differ.

cards.prompt: What is Proportional Allocation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Proportional allocation assigns stratum sample sizes proportional to stratum population sizes. With SRS within strata it yields the same sampling fraction across strata, before rounding and other constraints.
required_concepts: n_h proportional to N_h.
major_error_concepts: Calling equal numbers from unequal-sized strata proportional allocation.

cards.prompt: What is Neyman Allocation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For fixed total sample size and equal per-unit costs, Neyman allocation assigns n_h proportional to N_h S_h to minimize the stratified mean variance under the standard assumptions. More variable strata receive larger sampling fractions.
required_concepts: Allocate proportional to stratum size times standard deviation.
Equal-cost fixed-n setting.
major_error_concepts: Allocating using variance S_h squared instead of standard deviation in the Neyman formula.

cards.prompt: State the unconstrained continuous cost-optimal stratified allocation under a fixed linear sampling budget and its practical limits.
cards.definition: For independent within-stratum SRS, a fixed budget C=C_0+sum_h c_h n_h with C>C_0, known N_h and S_h>0, and unit costs c_h>0, the unconstrained continuous variance-minimizing allocation is n_h=(C-C_0)(N_h S_h/sqrt(c_h))/(sum_k N_k S_k sqrt(c_k)). Thus the direction is N_h S_h/sqrt(c_h). This interior rule assumes no active census or minimum-size bounds; practical allocations must respect integer sizes, n_h≤N_h, and other design constraints. A fixed-total-n problem is a different constraint.
required_concepts: State a fixed linear cost budget with positive unit costs.
Give the square-root-cost allocation and normalize it to the budget.
Recognize that bounds and integer sizes can change the unconstrained allocation.
major_error_concepts: The allocation N_h S_h/sqrt(c_h) is the exact integer optimum for any fixed total sample size, even if it assigns more samples than a stratum contains.

cards.prompt: What is Poststratification? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Poststratification adjusts an already selected sample to known population totals for defined groups. It differs from design stratification before selection and requires adequate sample support within adjustment groups.
required_concepts: After-selection alignment with known group totals.
Distinct from design stratification.
major_error_concepts: Claiming poststratification retroactively makes the original selection design stratified.

cards.prompt: What is Cluster Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Cluster sampling selects groups of units and then observes all or some units within selected groups. It can reduce collection cost but often reduces precision for positively correlated outcomes within clusters.
required_concepts: Select groups, then units within chosen groups.
Within-cluster similarity affects precision.
major_error_concepts: Assuming observing many members of one cluster is equivalent to spreading them across independent clusters.

cards.prompt: What is One-Stage Cluster Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: One-stage cluster sampling selects clusters and observes every eligible unit in each selected cluster. Design weights and variance must reflect cluster selection rather than treating the final units as an SRS automatically.
required_concepts: Select clusters and enumerate their units.
major_error_concepts: Calling a design one-stage when it additionally subsamples units inside selected clusters.

cards.prompt: What is Two-Stage Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Two-stage sampling first selects primary units and then samples secondary units within them. Final inclusion probabilities combine first-stage selection with conditional second-stage selection under the stated design.
required_concepts: Selection occurs at two nested stages.
Multiply appropriate stage probabilities.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring the first-stage selection probability in final weights.

cards.prompt: What is Primary Sampling Unit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A primary sampling unit is a unit selected at the first sampling stage, such as an area or institution. Independent replication for variance estimation often resides at this level rather than among every final respondent.
required_concepts: First-stage unit.
Important level for design variance.
major_error_concepts: Counting all respondents as independent PSUs in a clustered design.

cards.prompt: What is Secondary Sampling Unit? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A secondary sampling unit is selected within a sampled primary unit at the second stage. Its conditional selection probability must be distinguished from its overall population inclusion probability.
required_concepts: Second-stage selected unit.
Conditional versus overall selection probability.
major_error_concepts: Using its conditional second-stage probability alone as its final inclusion probability.

cards.prompt: What is Intracluster Correlation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Intracluster correlation measures similarity of outcomes among units within the same cluster relative to the model's total variability. Under a simple random-intercept model it is the between-cluster variance divided by total variance.
required_concepts: Within-cluster outcome similarity.
Variance-component ratio under the stated model.
major_error_concepts: Confusing cluster size with intracluster correlation.

cards.prompt: What is Cluster Design-Effect Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For equal cluster size m under a simple exchangeable correlation approximation, the clustering design effect is about 1+(m-1)rho. Unequal sizes, weighting, and other design features can change this approximation.
required_concepts: Approximate design effect 1+(m-1)rho.
Limited equal-size correlation assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Applying the approximation as an exact universal result for every multistage design.

cards.prompt: What is Number of Clusters and Precision? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Increasing the number of independently selected clusters often adds more information than increasing members per cluster when intracluster correlation is positive. Cost and minimum within-cluster measurement needs still affect allocation.
required_concepts: More independent clusters can improve precision efficiently under positive ICC.
major_error_concepts: Assuming doubling one cluster's respondents always equals doubling sampled clusters.

cards.prompt: What is Design Degrees of Freedom? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Survey inference degrees of freedom often depend on sampled PSUs and strata rather than just respondent count. With few independent PSUs, normal approximations and variance estimates can be unreliable even with many respondents.
required_concepts: Independent design units limit inferential replication.
major_error_concepts: Using thousands of clustered respondents as thousands of independent replication units.

cards.prompt: What is Probability Proportional to Size? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Probability proportional to size sampling uses an auxiliary size measure to make larger units more likely to be selected. Per-draw PPS probabilities and final inclusion probabilities must be distinguished, especially across replacement schemes.
required_concepts: Selection probability linked to a size measure.
Draw and inclusion probabilities may differ.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every PPS scheme has the same inclusion probability formula.

cards.prompt: What is Measure of Size? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A measure of size is an auxiliary nonnegative quantity used to guide PPS selection, such as an eligible-unit count. It should be defined and available on the frame; outdated or zero values can create coverage or efficiency problems.
required_concepts: Auxiliary size variable guides selection.
Frame quality and positive support matter.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any arbitrary size proxy guarantees optimal precision or complete coverage.

cards.prompt: What is Hansen-Hurwitz Estimator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For independent with-replacement draws with probabilities p_i, the Hansen-Hurwitz total estimator averages y_i/p_i over draws, counting repeat draws. It uses per-draw probabilities, unlike the distinct-unit Horvitz-Thompson estimator.
required_concepts: Average inverse-draw-probability expanded values.
Repeats counted as draws.
major_error_concepts: Replacing draw probabilities with final inclusion probabilities without changing the estimator.

cards.prompt: What is Systematic Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Systematic sampling chooses a random start and then selects regularly spaced entries in an ordered frame. Its inclusion and variance properties depend on interval, frame ordering, and design details; it is not automatically equivalent to SRS.
required_concepts: Random start plus regular selection interval.
Ordering affects behavior.
major_error_concepts: Dropping the random start while still claiming the same probability design.

cards.prompt: What is Periodicity in a Sampling Frame? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Periodicity risk occurs when a frame's repeating pattern aligns with the systematic sampling interval. The sample can then overrepresent particular pattern positions and have poor precision despite a random start.
required_concepts: Alignment of periodic frame structure and selection interval.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a random start removes every possible problem from a periodic ordered frame.

cards.prompt: What is Multistage Sampling Weight? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a nested multistage design, an ultimate unit's inclusion probability is the product of the appropriate conditional selection probabilities along its selection path. Final design weights invert that overall probability, with adjustments kept distinct.
required_concepts: Product of conditional stage probabilities.
Invert the overall probability.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying unconditional stage probabilities that do not represent the actual nested selection path.

cards.prompt: What is Horvitz-Thompson Estimator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Horvitz-Thompson total estimator is the sum over sampled distinct units of y_i/pi_i. With known positive inclusion probabilities it is design-unbiased for the population total before additional response or measurement problems.
required_concepts: Sum y_i/pi_i over selected distinct units.
Positive known inclusion probabilities.
major_error_concepts: Using unweighted values when inclusion probabilities differ while claiming the HT estimator.

cards.prompt: What is Horvitz-Thompson Mean? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: When population size N is known, dividing the Horvitz-Thompson total estimate by N estimates the finite-population mean without introducing a random denominator. Dividing instead by estimated population size gives a different ratio estimator.
required_concepts: HT total divided by known N.
Known and estimated denominators differ.
accepted_variants: HT mean estimator with known population size.
major_error_concepts: Equating fixed-denominator and random-denominator estimators in all samples.

cards.prompt: State the HT total variance and its standard unbiased sample estimator, including joint-inclusion and diagonal conventions.
cards.definition: For a fixed finite population, pi_i>0, and pi_ij=P(I_i=I_j=1) with pi_ii=pi_i, the HT total has variance V=sum_i sum_j (pi_ij-pi_i*pi_j)(y_i/pi_i)(y_j/pi_j). If all relevant pi_ij>0, an unbiased estimator is Vhat=sum_(i in s) sum_(j in s) [(pi_ij-pi_i*pi_j)/pi_ij](y_i/pi_i)(y_j/pi_j). The sums include diagonal terms. Positive marginal inclusion probabilities alone do not justify this estimator when joint probabilities vanish.
required_concepts: Give the covariance-of-inclusion formula for the HT total variance.
Give the sample double sum with division by pi_ij for an unbiased estimator under pairwise positivity.
Include diagonal terms using pi_ii=pi_i and distinguish marginal from joint positivity.
major_error_concepts: Replace every pi_ij by pi_i*pi_j in the HT variance, since inclusion indicators in every sampling design are independent.

cards.prompt: What is Hajek Mean Estimator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Hajek mean estimator divides the inverse-probability-weighted outcome sum by the sum of inverse-probability weights. This ratio can stabilize estimation but is not generally exactly design-unbiased in finite samples.
required_concepts: Weighted sum divided by total weight.
Generally a finite-sample biased ratio.
major_error_concepts: Claiming normalization preserves exact HT unbiasedness for every sample design.

cards.prompt: What is Ratio Estimation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A ratio estimator uses an estimated relation between an outcome and an auxiliary variable, often multiplying a sample ratio by a known population auxiliary total. It can improve precision when the relation is suitable but introduces ratio-estimation considerations.
required_concepts: Use an outcome-to-auxiliary ratio and known auxiliary information.
major_error_concepts: Using an auxiliary total that refers to a different target population without acknowledging the mismatch.

cards.prompt: What is Ratio-Estimator Bias? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Ratio-estimator bias arises because the expectation of a ratio need not equal the ratio of expectations. It often becomes small under suitable large-sample conditions but is not eliminated simply by unbiased numerator and denominator estimates.
required_concepts: Expectation does not commute with division.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a ratio of two unbiased estimators is automatically unbiased.

cards.prompt: What is Regression Estimation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Regression estimation uses auxiliary variables with known population information to improve estimation, adjusting an outcome total or mean by an estimated outcome-auxiliary relationship. Its design properties depend on how sampling weights and residual corrections are used.
required_concepts: Auxiliary relationships improve population estimation.
major_error_concepts: Treating any unweighted predictive regression as automatically a design-valid total estimator.

cards.prompt: What is Model-Assisted Inference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Model-assisted inference uses a working outcome model to improve a design-based estimator while retaining randomization-based justification under suitable conditions. It differs from inference resting entirely on the truth of a population model.
required_concepts: Working model aids efficiency within design-based reasoning.
major_error_concepts: Equating model-assisted and purely model-dependent inference without stating their different assumptions.

cards.prompt: What is Calibration Weighting? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Calibration weighting adjusts initial weights so weighted auxiliary totals match known population totals, subject to a chosen adjustment criterion. Matching those totals does not guarantee unbiasedness for every unmeasured outcome or selection mechanism.
required_concepts: Adjusted weights satisfy known auxiliary-total constraints.
Balance does not guarantee universal bias removal.
major_error_concepts: Claiming exact demographic balance proves every outcome estimate is unbiased.

cards.prompt: What is Raking? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Raking iteratively adjusts weights to match known marginal totals for several categorical variables. Matching margins does not necessarily match the full joint distribution, and sparse or empty cells can limit the procedure.
required_concepts: Iterative matching of marginal population totals.
Margins are not the full joint distribution.
major_error_concepts: Claiming raking on two separate margins necessarily matches every cross-classified cell.

cards.prompt: What is Weight Trimming? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Weight trimming limits extreme weights to reduce variance or instability. It changes the estimator and can introduce bias or break calibration constraints unless followed by an appropriate, disclosed adjustment.
required_concepts: Cap or reduce extreme weights.
Bias-variance and calibration tradeoffs.
major_error_concepts: Claiming trimming always improves accuracy without affecting bias or target balance.

cards.prompt: What is Weight-Only Effective Sample Size? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For positive weights, a common weight-only effective sample-size summary is (sum w)^2 divided by sum w squared. It reflects weight concentration but does not by itself incorporate clustering, outcome relationships, or selection bias.
required_concepts: Correct weight-concentration formula.
Not full design precision or bias assessment.
major_error_concepts: Treating this weight-only number as exact effective size for every outcome under any clustered design.

cards.prompt: Define an inverse-weighted-empirical-CDF quantile, including weight restrictions and tie handling.
cards.definition: For nonnegative weights w_i with W=sum_i w_i>0, define the weighted empirical CDF F_w(x)=sum_i w_i*1{y_i≤x}/W. An inverse-CDF weighted p-quantile, 0<p<1, is q_p=inf{x:F_w(x)≥p}; all tied observations at a value contribute together. This convention is stepwise; interpolation rules can define different estimators and should be named separately. Negative weights do not generally define a monotone CDF or this probability-quantile interpretation.
required_concepts: Normalize nonnegative weights with a positive total.
Include the entire mass at tied values using y_i≤x.
Specify the inverse-CDF threshold convention rather than silently choosing an interpolation rule.
major_error_concepts: Any signed survey weights define a valid empirical CDF, even if its cumulative value exceeds one or decreases as x increases.

cards.prompt: What is Survey Domain? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A domain is a subpopulation for which an estimate is desired, such as units with a specified characteristic. It can cross strata and clusters and need not have been a separate sampling stratum.
required_concepts: Subpopulation estimand.
Domain differs from design stratum.
major_error_concepts: Treating every analysis subgroup as a separately sampled stratum.

cards.prompt: What is Domain Variance Estimation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Domain estimation uses domain membership indicators within the full design so variance reflects how domain units were sampled. Simply deleting all nondomain records can discard needed PSU or stratum information in complex designs.
required_concepts: Preserve full design information for domain variance.
major_error_concepts: Assuming filtering records before defining the design always yields the correct subgroup variance.

cards.prompt: What is Taylor Linearization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Taylor linearization approximates a smooth nonlinear estimator by a linear expression whose design variance is easier to estimate. It is often used for ratios and regression summaries, with accuracy depending on regularity and sample support.
required_concepts: First-order linear approximation for design variance.
major_error_concepts: Calling linearization an exact variance formula for every nonlinear statistic and sample size.

cards.prompt: What is Replicate Weights? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Replicate weights encode repeated design-respecting perturbations of the survey sample. Recomputing the estimator under each replicate and applying the supplied scaling estimates variance, including specified weighting adjustments.
required_concepts: Repeated estimates using design-consistent replicate weights.
Replication scaling must match method.
major_error_concepts: Treating replicate weights as interchangeable ordinary respondent weights without method-specific scaling.

cards.prompt: What is Survey Jackknife? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A survey jackknife deletes or perturbs appropriate design units, often PSUs, to form replicate estimates. Its replicate construction and scale factors must reflect stratification and the actual design rather than blindly deleting individual respondents.
required_concepts: Delete or perturb design units to estimate variance.
major_error_concepts: Applying an IID respondent jackknife unchanged to a clustered multistage survey.

cards.prompt: What is Balanced Repeated Replication? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Balanced repeated replication forms balanced half-sample replicates in designs represented by two PSUs per variance stratum. Its weights and variance factors follow the replication construction; modified methods such as Fay's use partial perturbation.
required_concepts: Balanced PSU half-sample replicates under suitable strata representation.
major_error_concepts: Using half-sample replication without accounting for the PSU-stratum structure or scaling.

cards.prompt: What is Survey Bootstrap? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A survey bootstrap resamples units according to a construction that represents the original sampling design, often resampling PSUs within strata. An ordinary IID respondent bootstrap does not generally preserve a complex survey's dependence or selection structure.
required_concepts: Bootstrap must respect survey design.
Respondent IID resampling can be invalid.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring clustering and stratification while claiming design-consistent bootstrap variance.

cards.prompt: What is Single-PSU Stratum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A stratum with only one sampled PSU lacks direct within-stratum between-PSU replication for common variance estimators. Handling it requires a stated design justification or method, not silently assigning zero variance in every case.
required_concepts: Single PSU limits variance replication.
Explicit treatment required.
major_error_concepts: Assuming one sampled PSU necessarily means that stratum has no sampling uncertainty.

cards.prompt: What is Nonresponse? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Nonresponse occurs when selected eligible units or requested items are not observed. It is a post-selection missingness problem and can create bias when response relates to survey outcomes after any adjustment.
required_concepts: Missing information from selected eligible units.
Outcome-related response can bias estimates.
major_error_concepts: Equating a probability sampling design with guaranteed unbiasedness after selective nonresponse.

cards.prompt: What is Unit Nonresponse? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Unit nonresponse means an eligible selected unit provides no usable survey response for the designated response definition. It differs from item nonresponse within an otherwise participating unit.
required_concepts: Entire selected unit lacks usable response.
major_error_concepts: Calling one skipped question whole-unit nonresponse when other usable responses exist.

cards.prompt: What is Item Nonresponse? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Item nonresponse means a particular requested measurement is missing for a unit that otherwise supplies usable information. Different items can therefore have different response sets and missingness mechanisms.
required_concepts: Missing particular variable within a responding unit.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every variable has the same observed sample just because participants completed some survey items.

cards.prompt: What is Missing Completely at Random? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Missing completely at random means missingness is independent of the full relevant data, under the stated model. It is stronger than missing at random and is rarely justified solely by a low missingness percentage.
required_concepts: Missingness independent of observed and unobserved relevant values.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a small missing fraction proves MCAR.

cards.prompt: What is Missing at Random? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Missing at random means missingness depends only on observed data once the model's conditioning information is included. It can justify certain likelihood, weighting, or imputation methods with further assumptions, but does not mean data are missing haphazardly.
required_concepts: Conditional independence from missing values given observed information.
major_error_concepts: Defining MAR as missingness unrelated to every observed variable.

cards.prompt: What is Missing Not at Random? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Missing not at random means the missingness probability still depends on unobserved values after conditioning on the observed information in the model. The missing-value distribution is then generally not identified without additional assumptions or information.
required_concepts: Residual dependence on unobserved values.
Additional identification assumptions needed.
major_error_concepts: Claiming observed records alone universally identify the unseen outcomes under MNAR.

cards.prompt: What is Weighting-Class Adjustment? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A weighting-class nonresponse adjustment increases respondent weights within groups intended to have similar response and outcome behavior. It relies on adequate support and an assumption that respondents represent nonrespondents within adjustment classes.
required_concepts: Reweight respondents within suitable classes.
Within-class response assumption matters.
major_error_concepts: Claiming any arbitrary grouping automatically removes nonresponse bias.

cards.prompt: What is Response-Propensity Weighting? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A response-propensity adjustment estimates response probability from observed auxiliary variables and weights respondents inversely to that probability, usually alongside design weights. Validity depends on the response model, positivity, and the relevant missingness assumptions.
required_concepts: Inverse estimated response probability combined with design weighting.
Model and positive support assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Equating estimated response propensity with the original sample inclusion probability.

cards.prompt: What is Imputation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Imputation fills missing values using an explicit rule or predictive model. Single imputation does not by itself account for uncertainty in the missing values and may understate uncertainty if filled values are treated as known observations.
required_concepts: Fill missing entries under stated assumptions.
Account for missing-value uncertainty separately.
major_error_concepts: Treating all imputed values as known truths with no uncertainty.

cards.prompt: State the scalar multiple-imputation estimate and Rubin total-variance combining rule, noting what survey designs require.
cards.definition: Under proper-imputation and compatible-analysis assumptions, obtain scalar estimates Q_m and their complete-data variance estimates U_m from M≥2 completed datasets. Rubin combining rules use Qbar=(1/M)sum_m Q_m, W=(1/M)sum_m U_m, B=(1/(M-1))sum_m(Q_m-Qbar)^2, and total variance T=W+(1+1/M)B. For survey data, each U_m and the imputation model must respect the sampling design as needed. Replicate weights are one possible variance method, not a prerequisite to the definition of multiple imputation.
required_concepts: Combine estimates by their mean and distinguish within-imputation W from between-imputation B.
Use T=W+(1+1/M)B with at least two imputations under the stated compatibility assumptions.
Survey complete-data variances must respect the design; replication is not the only permitted method.
major_error_concepts: Average the completed datasets once and report only the complete-data variance, since multiple imputations eliminate missing-value uncertainty.

cards.prompt: What is Donor Imputation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A donor imputation method replaces missing values using observed values from suitably chosen similar units. Donor selection should reflect relevant predictors and design features; copying an observed value does not remove imputation uncertainty.
required_concepts: Use observed values from appropriate donors.
Donor choice and uncertainty matter.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an actual observed donor value is automatically the missing unit's true value.

cards.prompt: What is Missing-Data Sensitivity Analysis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Missing-data sensitivity analysis varies assumptions about unseen values or response mechanisms and examines how estimates change. It exposes dependence on untestable assumptions rather than proving one missingness model correct.
required_concepts: Vary plausible missingness or unseen-outcome assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Calling one MAR analysis a complete assessment of all MNAR risks.

cards.prompt: What is Measurement Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Measurement error is the difference between a recorded response and the intended true quantity under a defined measurement model. It can be random or systematic and is distinct from uncertainty about which units were sampled.
required_concepts: Recorded versus intended quantity discrepancy.
Distinct from selection error.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a census cannot have measurement error.

cards.prompt: What is Construct and Operational Measure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A construct is a concept a survey intends to measure, while an operational measure is the observable question, scale, or rule used to represent it. A convenient question does not automatically capture the full construct.
required_concepts: Distinguish concept from its observable measurement rule.
major_error_concepts: Equating any single proxy question with a complete and valid measurement of a broad construct.

cards.prompt: What is Neutral Question Wording? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A neutral survey question uses clear wording that does not push a respondent toward a preferred answer. It specifies the relevant referent and time period and avoids assuming facts the respondent may not accept.
required_concepts: Clear, nonleading wording with stated referent.
major_error_concepts: Using approval-seeking or loaded wording while claiming neutral measurement.

cards.prompt: What is Double-Barreled Question? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A double-barreled question asks about multiple distinct propositions but provides only one response. A respondent may agree with one part and disagree with another, making the resulting answer ambiguous.
required_concepts: Multiple propositions forced into one answer.
major_error_concepts: Treating agreement with a combined item as separate agreement with every component.

cards.prompt: What is Question-Order Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Question-order effects occur when earlier questions influence how later ones are interpreted or answered. Randomization or planned ordering can help assess or manage these context effects, but order must still suit comprehension and routing.
required_concepts: Earlier items alter later responses.
major_error_concepts: Assuming question order cannot affect answers because the wording of each item is unchanged.

cards.prompt: What is Survey Mode Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A mode effect is a measurement difference associated with how the survey is administered, such as interviewer, telephone, or self-completion modes. Observed differences can also reflect who responds in each mode, so measurement and selection should be separated.
required_concepts: Administration mode can change recorded answers.
Mode comparisons may also contain selection differences.
major_error_concepts: Attributing every difference between web and telephone respondents solely to question delivery.

cards.prompt: What is Recall Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Recall error occurs when respondents inaccurately remember or date past events. Specifying a feasible reference period and using suitable memory aids can help, but retrospective self-report is not automatically exact.
required_concepts: Errors in remembering past events or timing.
major_error_concepts: Assuming respondents accurately recall any event frequency regardless of elapsed time.

cards.prompt: What is Social-Desirability Bias? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Social-desirability bias occurs when respondents alter answers toward what they perceive as socially acceptable. Privacy of response and neutral administration can affect this mechanism, but cannot guarantee its elimination.
required_concepts: Responses shift toward perceived acceptable answers.
major_error_concepts: Assuming anonymous collection necessarily removes all social-desirability effects.

cards.prompt: What is Cognitive Interviewing? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Cognitive interviewing investigates how respondents understand a question, retrieve information, judge it, and choose an answer. It diagnoses measurement problems rather than estimating population percentages from a representative sample.
required_concepts: Study respondent interpretation and response process.
Not primarily population estimation.
major_error_concepts: Using a small cognitive-interview sample to claim a population proportion.

cards.prompt: What is Pilot Survey? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A pilot survey rehearses sampling, recruitment, questionnaire flow, collection, and processing on a limited scale. It identifies operational and measurement problems but does not alone establish final population representativeness or precise outcomes.
required_concepts: Small-scale rehearsal of survey procedures.
major_error_concepts: Calling successful pilot logistics proof of unbiased final survey estimates.

cards.prompt: What is Sampling and Nonsampling Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sampling error is random variation due to observing a sample instead of the entire population under the design. Nonsampling error includes coverage, nonresponse, measurement, and processing problems, some of which can persist in a census.
required_concepts: Selection variability versus other error sources.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every survey error shrinks at the usual square-root sample-size rate.

cards.prompt: What is Total Survey Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Total survey error is a framework combining multiple ways a survey estimate can depart from its target, including sampling, coverage, nonresponse, measurement, and processing. It motivates balancing effort across error sources rather than optimizing sample size alone.
required_concepts: Consider multiple error components jointly.
major_error_concepts: Equating a narrow sampling margin of error with low total survey error.

cards.prompt: What is Longitudinal Panel? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A longitudinal panel follows the same units over multiple waves. It supports within-unit change analysis but introduces repeated-measure dependence, attrition, and possible effects of prior participation.
required_concepts: Repeated observations on the same units.
Dependence and attrition matter.
major_error_concepts: Treating repeated responses from one unit as independent newly sampled units.

cards.prompt: What is Panel Attrition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Panel attrition is the loss of participating units over follow-up waves. It can change the panel's composition and bias longitudinal estimates when dropout relates to the outcomes or changes being studied.
required_concepts: Loss of units across follow-up.
Selective dropout affects inference.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the original probability sample remains representative after arbitrary attrition.

cards.prompt: What is Refreshment Sample? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A refreshment sample adds newly selected units to supplement a continuing panel. It can improve current-population coverage or provide information about attrition, but does not automatically identify every missing longitudinal outcome.
required_concepts: New sampled units supplement an existing panel.
Does not automatically recover missing histories.
major_error_concepts: Assuming new respondents supply the unobserved past responses of departed panel members.

cards.prompt: What is Panel Weighting Targets? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Cross-sectional panel weights target a population at one wave, while longitudinal weights target a defined population and participation pattern across waves. They can require different eligibility, response adjustments, and estimands.
required_concepts: One-wave and multiwave targets require different weights.
major_error_concepts: Using a single-wave weight for every longitudinal estimand without checking the target population.

cards.prompt: What is Survey Response Rate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A response rate summarizes the share of eligible sampled units that respond under a stated disposition rule. Unknown eligibility and partial responses require explicit handling, and a high rate alone does not prove absence of nonresponse bias.
required_concepts: Response fraction under explicit eligibility and disposition rules.
Rate alone does not establish bias.
major_error_concepts: Claiming any survey with a high response rate must have negligible bias.

cards.prompt: What is Representativeness? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Representativeness concerns whether a sample and estimation procedure support the intended population conclusions. Matching a few observed demographics or having many respondents does not alone establish representativeness for all outcomes.
required_concepts: Inference-specific population support.
Size and superficial balance are insufficient.
major_error_concepts: Calling a sample universally representative solely because its age distribution matches the population.

cards.prompt: What is Survey Methods Disclosure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Survey reporting should specify the population, frame, design, collection dates, response handling, estimator, weights, and design-aware uncertainty. These details distinguish a reproducible estimate from a percentage detached from its sampling and measurement context.
required_concepts: Disclose target, selection, response, weighting, and uncertainty.
major_error_concepts: Reporting only respondent count and a percentage as sufficient evidence of population validity.

cards.prompt: What is Survey Data Minimization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Data minimization limits collection and retention to information needed for the stated survey purpose. Identifiers and sensitive details can create disclosure risk without improving the estimand, so their necessity should be considered explicitly.
required_concepts: Collect and retain only purpose-relevant information.
major_error_concepts: Assuming more identifying data is automatically beneficial for statistical accuracy.

cards.prompt: What is Statistical Disclosure Risk? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Statistical disclosure risk is the possibility that released data reveal information about individual units, including through combinations of seemingly indirect attributes. Removing names alone does not guarantee that records or small aggregate cells are nonidentifying.
required_concepts: Individuals may be exposed through indirect or combined information.
major_error_concepts: Claiming deleting direct names always makes a detailed survey dataset anonymous.

cards.prompt: What is Finite Population and Superpopulation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Finite-population inference targets the defined current collection of units, whereas superpopulation inference targets parameters of a model generating possible populations. The inferential target and assumptions should be stated rather than silently interchanged.
required_concepts: Fixed population quantity versus model-generating parameter.
major_error_concepts: Assuming design-unbiasedness for one finite population alone establishes every superpopulation model claim.

cards.prompt: What is Duplicate Frame Entries? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Duplicate frame entries can give some units multiple opportunities for selection. A valid design must account for multiplicity in inclusion probabilities or resolve duplicates before selection without silently changing the target population.
required_concepts: Multiple entries can change selection chance.
Handle multiplicity or documented frame deduplication.
major_error_concepts: Treating duplicated units as having the same selection probability as unique units without checking the mechanism.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Sampling and Survey Methods.
